title: Ganesha Writes the Mahabharata
hook: Vyasa speaks, Ganesha writes: does the holy word live in the voice or on the page?
carry: shruti: holy words were heard before written
tomorrow: why would Rama eat fruit someone had already bitten?

segments.voice: Yesterday, atman: the self that makes anything dear, the treasure Maitreyi chose over a fortune. Today, an argument Hindus really have, and a god holding a pen.

Priya's dad says: just write Nani's line in English letters, she knows it by heart anyway. He has a point, and it's an old one. For many centuries the Vedas, Hinduism's oldest scriptures, weren't read from pages at all. They were heard: recited by a teacher, repeated by a student, word for word, generation after generation. So which is the scripture, the voice or the page?
screen: `JUST USE ENGLISH LETTERS.` → `THE VEDAS WERE HEARD.` → `THE VOICE OR THE PAGE?`

segments.voice: One side says the voice. The Vedas are called shruti, what is heard. Tradition says the ancient seers didn't make them up; they heard them. And they're still taught mouth to ear, with chanting patterns that repeat the words forward, backward and in pairs so not a syllable slips. Many Hindus would say a mantra lives in its sound, and the letters of any alphabet are only its clothes. The other side says the page matters too, and it has a god on its side. In a favorite telling, the sage Vyasa needed a scribe for the Mahabharata, and Ganesha agreed on one condition: Vyasa must never pause. Vyasa added his own: Ganesha must understand every verse before he writes it. So whenever Vyasa needed a breath, he spoke a knotty verse, and Ganesha had to stop and think. Some tellings add that when the pen broke, Ganesha snapped off his own tusk and kept writing. That's one reason he's shown holding a broken tusk, and why many Hindus write a line to Ganesha at the top of a new page. Under the debate is a real teaching. Shruti is what was heard, the Vedas. Smriti, what is remembered, the epics, the Gita, the law books, came after and is taught as resting on it. Both lived in voices long before ink, and writing them down is a way to serve them. So Priya can do both. The script carries the line's sound faithfully. Nani's voice carries the line itself.
screen: `SHRUTI: WHAT IS HEARD.` · `TAUGHT MOUTH TO EAR.` · `VYASA SPEAKS. GANESHA WRITES.` · `SMRITI: WHAT IS REMEMBERED.` · then, large: `WRITING SERVES THE SOUND.`

segments.voice: If you know a short prayer or mantra, say it once softly, then once only in your mind, and notice it's still whole without a page. If you don't pray, use any line you know by heart, a song or a blessing. Then sit in the quiet after, with the sound still there.
Devanagari: one of the scripts that has carried Sanskrit's holy sound onto the page, the way Ganesha carried Vyasa's.
Keep this: shruti. Holy words were heard before they were written, and the page still serves the voice. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vedic chanting is still taught orally, teacher to student, in traditional schools; and many Hindus write 'Shri Ganeshaya namah' at the top of a new page or account book before they begin.

fork.setup: your dad says a mantra written in English letters isn't 'real'. your cousin says the letters don't matter at all. what's the fairest answer from the tradition?
options: the mantra lives in its sound; any careful script can carry it, and Devanagari carries the sound closely.
only Devanagari is holy; other letters break the mantra.
neither matters; a mantra is just words.
fork.reveal: the Vedas are shruti, what is heard: the sound comes first. scripts serve it, some more exactly than others.
